segments.title: The claim and the locked rule
sections: Why Most Trading Advice Cannot Be Checked
Lock The Rule Before You Look

cues.text: A setup never fails. A level always holds. A pattern prints money.
You have heard all three. Notice what is missing: the rule, when it was written down, what it was compared against, and how many times it was tried.
Without those four things there is nothing to check. All that is left is how confident the person sounds. Confidence is free, which is why there is so much of it.
Now, what a claim you can check looks like.
One: a rule stated exactly enough that someone else could run it.
Two: a record of when the rule was fixed.
Three: a comparison that could have made it look bad.
Four: results from conditions that were not used to build it.
The first habit: lock the rule before you look.
Write the rule down in full before you open the data.
The entry. The stop, the order that closes the trade when you are wrong. The target, the price the trade aims for.
And when the rule applies, and when it does not.
A rule written in full, and dated, before the data is opened is called a locked rule.
Reverse the order and you have fitted the rule to the data. A fitted rule always looks good on the data that made it. It tells you nothing about your next session.
The rule: write the whole rule down before you open the data, and the data gets a fair chance to say no.
Getting it wrong is writing the rule after you have looked. You will find a version that would have looked good, because the chart already holds the answer.
That tells you what the chart did. It does not tell you what the rule does.

segments.title: The null and the two halves
sections: Split The Sample, And Look At Recent Data Separately

cues.text: A result needs something to be compared with.
That something is a null: the same locked rule, run on price paths that have been shuffled.
Each session's one-minute price changes are reshuffled inside thirty-minute blocks. That destroys any real sequence and keeps the session's volatility, how much price moved.
Think of the null as the weather: what the market was going to do anyway.
Run the rule on the null many times over. The average of those runs is the baseline.
Two terms before the next one. Expectancy is the average result per trade, in R. R is the amount you risked, so a result of two R is twice what you risked.
Now, edge. Edge is a rule's expectancy after costs, above what the same rule earns on its null.
The rule: if the rule does no better on the real data than on its null, it has no edge.
Markets drift, and ranges expand and contract. A rising tide lifts every boat. The boat did not do that.
Next, split the sample. The sample is every trade the rule took in the test.
Divide it in half and check both halves.
Positive in one half and negative in the other is not an edge. It is one good stretch and one bad one, and you cannot tell which is the exception.
Then look at recent data on its own. A rule that worked in conditions that no longer exist is history, not a tool.
Put together, the null, the two halves, the calendar years and the recent data make one test. It is called Gate 1.
Gate 1 is the test of a locked rule on historical market data. It passes on four things.
One: at least one hundred trades.
Two: it beats the null.
Three: it is positive in both halves and in each calendar year.
Four: a recency check, on 2023 to 2026.
You report the result in R, with four numbers: how many trades, the share that won, the expectancy, and the null's expectancy beside it.
Getting it wrong is reading one total. Each split is one more chance to fail, and a result that survives all of them is worth more than one shown only in aggregate.

segments.title: Your execution and simulated fills
sections: Why Simulated Fills Cannot Measure Edge

cues.text: A backtest is your rule run on past market data. It assumes a perfect trader.
It takes every signal, every time the rule says trade, at the stated price, without hesitation. You do not. You skip some signals, hesitate on others, and place orders a little differently each time.
The backtest never flinches. It also never traded.
So keep your own executions in their own count, apart from any backtest. Never blend the two.
The market data answers one question: did the market behave that way. Your record answers another: can you collect on it. The two answers are independent.
The rule: a rule that tests well and that you cannot execute is not yours yet.
Your record has its own test. It is called Gate 2.
Gate 2 is the test of your own live trades of a rule. Live means real orders in a real market. It passes on three things.
One: at least thirty live trades.
Two: across at least twenty distinct sessions.
Three: expectancy of at least 0.3 R after commissions.
Sim trades never count toward it. Sim is the simulator, the practice mode on your platform, and the next chapter is why.
Now, simulated fills.
A limit order is an order to buy or sell at your price or better. The simulator fills it the moment price touches your price. Real markets do not always fill you there.
Price can touch your level, the price you planned to trade at, then turn around and never fill you. The trades that get away are often the best ones.
Where in the level you get filled is the variable that decides whether a trade pays, and the simulator ignores it.
The rule for sim: it tells you how often something happened. It cannot tell you whether you would have been paid for it.
Getting it wrong is counting sim trades as evidence. Keep sim as practice, and as a count of occurrences, never as evidence of edge.

segments.title: Small samples, and this course too
sections: Apply It To This Course Too

cues.text: A small run of trades feels like information. Mostly it is noise.
A few wins in a row prove little. So do a few losses.
The count is not the whole story either. Thirty trades across four sessions is one week's conditions, not a sample.
If those sessions trended, every trade looked like a trend trade. If they were quiet, nothing followed through. Thirty trades in one mood is a large sample of a small thing.
The rule: you need trades spread across many different days and conditions, so that no single kind of market does all the work.
Getting it wrong is counting trades and not sessions. That is why Gate 2 asks for twenty distinct sessions as well as thirty trades.
Now, one question to ask of any claim.
What would have to be true for this to be wrong, and has that been checked?
If nobody can say what would count as wrong, the claim cannot be tested. If they can, and it has not been checked, it is an idea, not a result.
That includes this course.
Read every claim through the same lens. One: a rule stated before it was tested.
Two: compared with a null.
Three: checked in separate halves and in recent data.
Four: kept apart from your own execution record.
This course gives you setups. A setup is a level and a read together: where you trade, and what price has to do there.
It gives you rules and routines too. It does not give you results. Whether any of them holds for you is decided by your own record.
So, what to do with them. Treat each one as a testable idea.
Write the rule down, log every instance, and be suspicious of anyone, this site included, who tells you a trading idea is settled.

cues.text: Take one claim. A setup you trade, one you have been told about, or a rule on this site.
Score it. One point for each line that is true.
One: the rule is written exactly enough that someone else could run it.
Two: the rule was fixed before anyone looked at the data it was tested on.
Three: it was compared with a null, and beat it.
Four: it was positive in both halves of the sample and in recent data on its own.
Five: live trades of it are counted apart from the backtest, with sim left out.
The threshold. If line one or line two is missing, the claim cannot be checked at all. It is an opinion, and you set it aside.
With both, anything under five of five is an idea that has not had its test yet, and you treat it as one. You log it. You do not size it as a result.
Getting it wrong is skipping the date. A rule with no date on it was probably written after the chart.
After the chart, every rule is right. That is why the date goes on first.

cues.text: Your assignment. Before your next session, write one rule you trade, or want to trade, as one sentence.
Entry, stop, target, and when it applies. Then put the date beside it. That is the whole assignment.
Think of the date as a receipt. Dull to keep. It is also the only thing anyone accepts later.
Getting it wrong is writing a sentence nobody else could run. If another trader could not take the same trades from your sentence alone, it is not a rule yet. Rewrite it until they could.
The summary. A claim can be checked when its rule was written in full, and dated, before the data was opened.
Then it has to beat its null, hold in both halves and in recent data, and show up in your own live trades, counted apart, with sim left out.
Where it goes next. The dated rule becomes a line you log every instance of, with its outcome in R, in the journal: Module 18, Journaling and Review.
Every trade you log is a point in the count Gate 2 reads.
Module 21, Reading A Probability, teaches you to read a rate with its sample size beside it.
Module 22, How To Test An Edge, walks a locked rule through Gate 1 and Gate 2 on your own data.
